summary: The annealed 3Cr strip is the 3 wt% Cr member of the near-rapidly-solidified Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9) austenitic low-density steel strip series, produced by centrifugal casting and subsequently annealed in vacuum at 550 °C for 5 h. The work asks how Cr addition (0–9 wt%) modifies microstructure, carbide formation and mechanical properties of high-Mn, high-C low-density strips, and how a 550 °C/5 h anneal re-balances strength and ductility. For this strip the anneal raises yield strength (to 768 ± 9 MPa) while — unusually, and contrary to the Cr-free strip — also raising total elongation (to 37.4 ± 5 %), an effect traced to suppressed κ-carbide precipitation and to recovery of the high dislocation density inherited from near-rapid solidification.
composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al–1.2C–3Cr (wt%). Measured composition by ICP (Table 1) is Fe balance, Mn 27.6, Al 8.4, C 1.3, Cr 2.8 wt% — the measured Cr is close to the 3 wt% nominal target, and Mn/Al/C fall within the spans of the series (Mn 26.6–29.1, Al 8.4–9.9, C 1.2–1.3 wt%). Iron is the base element; Mn (with C) stabilizes austenite and secures ductility, C provides solid-solution strengthening and κ-carbide precipitation strengthening, Al lowers density, and Cr is the variable addition examined for its effect on κ-carbide precipitation, ferrite fraction and corrosion resistance. The parent alloy was melted from high-purity Fe (99.99%), Mn (99.9%), Al (99.9%), C (99.8%) and Cr (99.9%).
processing: Processing lineage: (1) parent near-rapid solidification / casting — the ingot was reheated to melt with an induction coil and the liquid metal was poured into a copper mold rotating at 600 r/min under Ar atmosphere, giving a calculated maximum cooling rate of about 5×10^3 K/s and strip dimensions of (60–80) mm × 60 mm × 2.5 mm; this as-cast 3Cr strip is the precursor of the present sample. (2) heat treatment — the strip was annealed in a vacuum electric resistance furnace at 550 °C for 5 h, which defines the annealed 3Cr strip. No cooling medium or heating/cooling rate is reported for the anneal. The 550 °C/5 h condition is one point of a 550 °C annealing-time series (1, 5 and 9 h) run on the 3Cr alloy.
microstructure: After annealing at 550 °C for 5 h the 3Cr strip still consists of an austenite (γ, FCC) matrix plus δ-ferrite (BCC); the ferrite size and fraction are essentially unchanged from the as-cast state (11.4 vol% ferrite measured for the as-cast 3Cr strip). δ-ferrite appears as dispersed second-phase particles in the austenite matrix, showing fine dots plus short elongated/angular fragments. SEM of the annealed strip shows a smooth grey matrix with dispersed dark second-phase particles and no resolvable grain boundary or dendritic network — in contrast to the annealed 0Cr strip, whose dendritic structure and grain boundaries remain clearly visible, an observation the authors link to improved corrosion resistance with Cr addition. κ-carbide precipitation remains suppressed: the austenite SADP superlattice is very weak and no κ(111) reflection (~41.4°) is seen in XRD, whereas it appears in the annealed Cr-free strip. Nano-scale DO3 ordered domains are present in the δ-ferrite (DO3 superlattice reflections in annealed 0Cr and 3Cr ferrite dark-field images), a feature absent from the as-cast 0Cr and 3Cr strips. The austenite dislocation density of the annealed 3Cr strip is clearly reduced relative to the as-cast 3Cr strip but is still higher than that of the annealed 0Cr strip.
properties: Tensile testing at a strain rate of 1 × 10^-3 s^-1 on specimens with a 20 mm × 4 mm × 1 mm gauge (MTS Criterion Model 44, 10 kN), values averaged over 3 measurements: yield strength 768 ± 9 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 915 ± 23 MPa, total elongation 37.4 ± 5 %. Relative to the as-cast 3Cr strip, annealing gives a yield-strength increment of +151 MPa and a total-elongation increment of +4.2 %. The reduction in strain-hardening rate of the annealed 3Cr strip relative to its as-cast state is the largest of the series, about 500 MPa; among the annealed strips, the strain-hardening rate increases with Cr content. Measured density of the 3Cr strip is 6.45 g/cm³ (SJ-600G electronic water-displacement density analyzer). Characterization techniques applied to this material include OM (Zeiss Axio Imager A2m), SEM, TEM (JEM-2100F, 200 kV) with BF/DF imaging and SADP, XRD (D/Max-2200, Cu target, 40 kV/40 mA, 4°/min) and ICP mass spectrometry for composition, plus room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing with engineering and true stress–strain and strain-hardening-rate curves.
mechanisms: Near-rapid solidification follows the FA mode L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → δ+γ: δ-ferrite nucleates and grows first from the melt, so ferrite remains dispersed inside the austenite grains of the strips, and increasing Cr raises the ferrite fraction and coarsens/blockifies the ferrite particles.

Cr addition expands the solid solubility of Al and C in Fe–Mn–Al–C and thereby lowers the driving force for κ-carbide formation, so κ-carbide precipitation is progressively suppressed: 3Cr (and 6Cr) austenite shows only a very weak κ superlattice and no κ(111) XRD peak, whereas the Cr-free strip shows a clear κ superlattice and κ(111) reflection.

Annealing at 550 °C for 5 h promotes κ-carbide precipitation (evidenced by the growing κ(111) peak and superlattice in 0Cr), and because κ-carbides raise the yield strength, all strips — including 3Cr, whose yield strength increases by +151 MPa — harden upon annealing; in 3Cr the carbide content and size nevertheless stay below those of the Cr-free strip.

Cr-containing strips carry a higher dislocation density than the Cr-free strip because suppressing nano-scale κ-carbides removes obstacles to dislocation formation under the same thermal stress imposed by rapid cooling; the higher strain-hardening rate of the Cr-containing strips corroborates this higher dislocation-formation ability.

Annealing at 550 °C for 5 h causes recovery: the dislocation density in the austenite of the Cr-containing strips is clearly reduced relative to their as-cast state, and this reduction of dislocations (together with the small increment of κ-carbide precipitation) is what raises the total elongation of the annealed 3Cr and 6Cr strips above their as-cast values.

Nano-scale κ-carbides cause glide-plane softening, which lowers the strain-hardening rate of the as-cast Cr-free strip; conversely, the reduced κ-carbide precipitation in Cr-containing strips allows slip bands to form during deformation and yields a high strain-hardening rate, so the annealed 3Cr strip shows a large (~500 MPa) drop in strain-hardening rate relative to its as-cast state.
Increased δ-ferrite fraction in Cr-containing strips adds phase-interface area that blocks dislocation propagation, which contributes to the loss of plasticity of the as-cast Cr-containing strips.

In the annealed strips DO3-ordered domains develop in the δ-ferrite (DO3 superlattice reflections appear in 0Cr and 3Cr only after annealing), indicating that the 550 °C/5 h treatment also orders the ferrite.

Initial dislocation density, not only the ability to form slip bands during deformation, controls elongation in this austenitic low-density steel: a high pre-existing dislocation density (as in as-cast Cr-containing strips) interferes with the usual finer-slip-band/higher-ductility relationship and lowers elongation.
conclusions: The annealed 3Cr strip illustrates the study's central finding that Cr addition and annealing interact strongly in Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr strips. Annealing at 550 °C for 5 h raises the yield strength of every strip by promoting κ-carbide precipitation, but the ductility change is opposite for Cr-free and Cr-containing strips: the Cr-free strip loses elongation (30.1 ± 2 % vs 40.8 ± 8 % as-cast) whereas every Cr-containing strip gains elongation — the annealed 3Cr strip reaches 37.4 ± 5 % (increment +4.2 %) and the annealed 6Cr strip even exceeds the annealed Cr-free strip. The gain is attributed to reduced dislocation density and the still-limited κ-carbide content/size in the Cr-bearing strips. The 3Cr strip also shows the largest strain-hardening-rate reduction (~500 MPa) upon annealing. Overall the series shows that Cr additions of 3 and 6 wt% can convert the anneal from a strength-for-ductility trade-off into a simultaneous strength-and-ductility improvement, whereas 9 wt% Cr forms grain-boundary Cr23C6 that makes the as-cast and annealed 9Cr strips the least ductile. The work demonstrates that near-rapid solidification centrifugal casting of thin strips combined with a 550 °C anneal is a viable near-net-shape route to high-strength, ductile austenitic low-density steels, provided the annealing time is optimized to balance κ-carbide coarsening against dislocation recovery.
unmapped: The slip-band spacing/width analysis and the dynamic slip band refinement (DSBR) discussion (Fig. 12 and Fig. 13: average slip-band spacing ~90 nm for as-cast 0Cr, ~190 nm for annealed 0Cr, ~80 nm for as-cast 6Cr, ~60 nm for annealed 6Cr; average slip-band widths 13.4 nm, 20.5 nm, 12.5 nm and 7.9 nm respectively) was performed only on the 0Cr and 6Cr strips after tensile fracture, not on the 3Cr strip, so no slip-band values can be assigned to this sample.

The 550 °C annealing-time study (1, 5 and 9 h, Fig. 11) was carried out on the 3Cr alloy; the 5 h condition corresponds to this sample, for which the annealing time series showed that κ-carbides precipitate mainly in the first hour while dislocation recovery needs longer, and that a longer anneal further improves plasticity at this temperature.

The observation that annealed Cr-containing strips (including 3Cr) no longer show resolvable grain boundaries or dendritic structure in SEM, unlike the annealed 0Cr strip, is discussed in the paper as evidence that Cr addition improves the corrosion resistance of the strips.
